utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the case for hearing be called.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-87/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning to everybody. Ms. Kravetz, you're ready for your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The first Prosecution witness is Mr. Veton Surroi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I would like to introduce Mr. Eliott Behar and next to him is Ms. Silvia D'Ascoli, who will be appearing before Your Honours later on in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think one of those names is entirely new to me and not yet appearing on any of the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, if it please you. May I just mention one matter briefly while the witness is being brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the witness list for the first week, I think we have Mustafa Draga as the last witness, and on the witness list for the next witness we have Shyhrete Berisha as the first witness. For scheduling purposes, I was wondering if there would be a problem, if there would be too much inconvenience, if we put Shyhrete Berisha before Mr. Draga, so it would just be a switch-around of those two witnesses who are coming next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Merely and interchange of those two witnesses in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would make for a more logical presentation because the witnesses would be dealing with the same issues, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, come in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No difficulty is foreseen with that at the present time, so you can proceed on that basis, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the card that is given to you now and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. I believe Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: My name is Veton Surroi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Surroi?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of July, 1961.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In Prishtina, Republic of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to go briefly through some facts of your personal background, and I'm just going to ask you to confirm to some facts. You're a Kosovo Albanian, son of a Yugoslav diplomatic, and during some years of your youth, you lived abroad in central and South America; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have a bachelors degree in philosophy and letters and by profession you're a journalist and publisher.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During your years in Kosovo you have been actively involved in politics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you have also been a member of several different Kosovo Albanian delegations that have been involved in international negotiations with regard to the status of Kosovo province?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I mentioned you had been living abroad for some years of your youth. You returned to Kosovo in 1982 and have been living there ever since?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation, Mr. Surroi?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At present I deal with the publishing of books. I work with a publishing house called Koha, and I am head of the board of the Foreign Policy Club.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During your political career were you also a member of the Kosovo Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I would like to ask you some questions about events that took plays in Kosovo in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and I would like to focus first that events that took place in 1989. Up until 1989, was the province of Kosovo autonomous province within the federal republic -- Yugoslav federation?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. Up until 1989, Kosova had the status of autonomy, with veto rights within the Federation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When was Kosovo granted this autonomous status?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: With the constitutional changes of 1968 and then the constitution of 1974, Kosova became an equal subject in the Yugoslav federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did this autonomous status of the province mean that Kosovo had its known institutions - police, judiciary - that operated separately from those of the federal and republican level?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: With the constitution of 1974, Kosova had all the institutions, its own institutions, which were similar or equal to the ones that the other republics in the Yugoslav federation had. And this meant institutions of internal affairs, such as the police, the secret police, and also foreign representation. They had a secretariat for foreign relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in March of 1989, did the Serbian Assembly propose a series of amendments to the 1974 constitution that you referred to which effectively revoked the autonomy of Kosovo as a province?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From 1982, Serbia began to exercise political pressure for changes to the constitution of Kosova, and this situation escalated in 1987, 1988, and 1989. The pressure was to make those amendments that would revoke the elements of equality in the status of Kosova so that Kosova would be subordinated to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in March of 1989, were these proposed amendments voted upon in the Kosovo Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, that's what they were called, they were voted. But it was not so because all around the parliament building that day there were APCs surrounding it. There was pressure against the whole population in Kosova, but especially against the MPs. And within the building there were people voting who were not members of the Assembly of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you already working as a journalist at the time in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I was a journalist working for the Rilindija newspaper, but I also used to write for Croatian and Serbia newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you cover the events surrounding or the circumstances surrounding this vote at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, I described the events, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the result of the vote that took place in 1989 at the assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The result was such that it would change the character of the constitution of Kosova and would place Kosova under its -- under the subordination of Serbia and its constitution and legal institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And some days later after this vote that you're referring to took place, were these amendments also voted upon by the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the result of the vote before the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, the result was the same, so the Serbian authorities proclaimed that Serbia at last had become one. It was united, unified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: As a result of these amendments that were passed or voted upon, were a series of special measures implemented which affected daily life in Kosovo for Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From that moment on, Serbia undertook a series of administrative measures. From 1989 to 1990, Kosova experienced a series of special measures that limited not only decision-making in Kosova but also limited the -- and restricted the everyday life of citizens in Kosova. I would illustrate this with measures in the security area. In 1989, they started to apply the measure of isolation as they called it. Over 200 citizens of Kosova were brought in by the police, and they were sent to Serbian prisons, kept there for 60 days without any legal assistance, and they were ill-treated physically. These were people who, in one way or another, had -- were prominent people. They were not political activists as such, but they were prominent people and had been in demonstrations, and so on. Then in 1990, the existing legal order that existed in Kosova was revoked, was suspended, and Kosova lost all its attributions. Even this legal situation that was created from Serbia was suspended. Everything was suspended. The institutions of the assembly, the radio and television of Prishtina, they were closed down, and also the Rilindija newspaper was shut down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I clarify your answer. You referred to the arrest of over 200 citizens of Kosovo. Were these persons belonging to certain ethnicity or were they from different ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: All of them were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, just to understand the impact of these special measures in daily life, could you explain how they affected the access to employment for persons of Kosovo Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After these changes, two kinds of pressure were being exercised. There was social -- there were social- or state-owned enterprises and those were forcefully integrated within the economic system of Serbia. And at the same time, the Albanian workers and employees were offered a kind of statement that they had to sign where they declared their loyalty to the institutions of Serbia. Those who refused to sign such a piece of paper, they were expelled or fired. This happened almost to all the Albanian workers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you're referring specifically to civil servants in public institutions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Not only public institutions but also economic enterprises. So, for example, you could be a manual worker in a factory that was state-owned, but even this manual worker had to sign a piece of paper where it said that he was a loyal person to the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And those who refused to sign were not allowed to remain in their jobs?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: All of them, no exception. The people who did not sign the piece of paper, all of them were fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What about the police? Were Kosovo Albanians allowed to be part of the police?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Especially the policemen at that time were under a lot of pressure to declare their loyalty to the institutions of Serbia, and the absolute majority of the Albanian policemen refused to do that, and they were fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did these special measures have any impact on the access of Kosovo Albanians to housing and to property?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were some other special measures as well at the time, and one of these measures was that selling and buying between ethnicities was not allowed, was forbidden. So Albanians could not buy from Serbs, any property from Serbs. This was one of those special measures. In the meantime, a number of Albanians who had flats that they owned, but they were called socially-owned -- it's a different system. It's a flat that was given to them by the company they worked in, for example. And these flats were taken from them, maybe not from all of them but a great number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you perceive what was the purpose of this specific measure of the restrictions to having access to buying property?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was clear. Serbia declared that they would never allow the number of Serbs to go down. They wanted the number of Serbs to increase in Kosova. And at that time, alongside the -- not allowing the selling and the buying of property, there were people coming from Serbia and Croatia, refugees, who were settling in Kosova in special settlements for refugees. And this was all for the purpose of changing the ethnic structure in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at the time, just roughly speaking, what was the ethnic composition of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Although it did not have clear statistics, what transpired from the census, which was not complete - and this census was conducted by the Serbian authorities at the time - I think that about 85 percent or something over that were Albanians and about 15 percent were Serbs and other ethnicities, non-Albanian ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And did these measures have any impact on the official languages that were used in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Up until 1989, there was a more satisfactory level of equality, if I may call it so, between the use of the Albanian language and the Serbo-Croat language in Kosova. After 1989, in public notices or communications, the Serbian language was used as an official language at the detriment of the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did these measures have any impact on the access of Kosovo Albanians to education?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After 1990 the right of Albanians to education was restricted dramatically. The Prishtina university was closed down, which at the time was called "Nest of Nationalism," and almost all the secondary schools were closed. So there was no access to secondary schools for Albanian pupils. In the primary level there was a clear segregation where the public means were given to primary schools that taught in Serbian, while the Albanian education system was mainly conducted in a parallel way to the existing Serbian system, what was called at the time the parallel primary school system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've referred to the parallel primary school system. Could you elaborate a bit on what you mean by that, the existing of the parallel school system?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In 1990, by the end of summer when we were faced with the fact that we would not have access, or the Albanian pupils would not have access to secondary education and tertiary university education, and the funding of Albanian education was being suspended by the Serbian authorities because the education system was dependent on the Serbian authorities, of course. What was called the Consultative Council of Political Parties in Kosova, the Albanian political parties in Kosova where I was a member of as well and at the proposal of Professor Agani and Mr. Rugova took the position of creating a parallel system of funding the education which would be dependent on the voluntary contributions of citizens; so that we would be able to have primary education in the existing primary school buildings, a secondary education in private buildings; but the teaching staff would be people who had been teachers in those secondary schools. And also the same thing would be done with the university education, so it would be based in private homes and then the citizens would contribute to finance them. So in this situation of parallel education system, all the generations from 1990 to 1999, that was the way -- how pupils and the young people would be educated, in this parallel system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred a bit earlier to Professor Agani. Could you tell us who Professor Agani was?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Professor Agani was vice-president of the LDK, which was the largest party. He was an ideologist of the Democratic League of Kosova. But not only that, but he was the person who had created the non-violent Albanian movement of that -- of those years. He was well-respected in Kosova but also in Belgrade and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You also referred to Mr. Rugova. Just very briefly, who was Mr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Dr. Rugova at the time was president of the Democratic League of Kosova. He was also leader of the peaceful movement in Kosova. He was that during all that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These special measures that you've been referring to, until when did they remain in force?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: They remained in force until the arrival of the NATO troops in -- on the 11th of June, 1999, at a time when the legal order established by the Serb authorities in 1989 was suspended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, going back to the early 1990s, in July 1990 was there a declaration made in the Kosovo parliament by members of the parliament regarding the status of the province?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In July 1990, keeping in mind the dramatic developments and the dissolution of Yugoslavia, members of the Kosovan Assembly, I would say devoted members of the assembly who had the interests of Kosova at their heart, in consultation amongst themselves and with the intellectual elite, decided to take a stand with regard to the position of Kosova and its future, and they made this constitutional declaration. They decided to declare Kosova a republic within the Yugoslav federation. This declaration had to be followed up with other legal decisions that would change Kosova into an equal republic to the other republics, and then with the dissolution of Yugoslavia, that would lead to an independent Kosova, just like the other independent republics that came out of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In the following year, in September 1991, was there a referendum in Kosovo regarding the independence status of the province?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After the referendums organised in Slovenia and Croatia, the consultative council took the decision to organise a referendum on independence, the independence of Kosova, so that the will of the citizens of Kosova would be expressed with regard to these developments and the movement and the tendency was clear towards -- it was toward the creation of independent states.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the result of the referendum in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The result was an absolute yes for an autonomous Kosova and with the possibility for it to become an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this referendum recognised by -- the results of the referendum recognised or accepted by Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. Serbia tried to hinder the referendum process, but in the end, the authorities in Serbia just rejected the result.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: On May 1992 were elections held for an assembly and a president of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Again, after the referendum we decided to hold parallel elections for our institutions. It was clear that we needed democratic legitimacy and institutions, and for that reason we held those elections and with -- President Rugova was elected with an absolute majority. The same happened with other institutions. These elections also were -- the result of these elections was also the government of Kosova and the people who were at that time persecuted by the Serbian authorities were obliged to go into exile.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who were these people that you're referring to that were persecuted by Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In the beginning there was Dr. Bujar Bukoshi. Earlier he had been kidnapped by the Serbian police before he became prime minister. He was nominated prime minister of Kosova. And then the other members of the government who were appointed were obliged to go abroad into exile. Some of them left just because they were afraid that they would have repercussions from the Serbian authorities, not because they had been persecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Kosovo Albanian population generally with respect to the special measures that were limited by Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The citizens of Kosova tried to resist these measures in the beginning by holding demonstrations. They were peaceful demonstrations, but they were suppressed. And in January 1990, we had a series of demonstrations of citizens. Also in February, there were people who died in those demonstrations. These were unarmed people that were killed by the Serbian police. And after this wave of protests of this nature, and with the organisation of political parties, an organised resistance began with the creation of parallel structures. The citizens of Kosova, in their absolute majority, never accepted the established of the Serbian power in the country. In the beginning, the resistance was peaceful, but then by the end it became an armed resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to this resistance becoming an armed resistance. Did some sectors of Kosovo Albanian society organise themselves to confront or fight against the presence of Serbian authorities in the province?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: My opinion is that after the Dayton Accords, where the Bosnian issue was discussed and the cease-fire in Bosnia as well, the Kosovan issue was not discussed there. So part of the segments of the Kosovan society began to organise themselves and get armed; and from this movement the KLA was created, and they had more dynamic activities after the winter of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And by "KLA," I understand you mean the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When was the KLA formed?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, there might be different interpretations on this, but I think that the KLA came out publicly on the 28th of November 1997, and they appeared there in uniform, in their uniform. So that's what I take as the real date of their coming out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, going back to an issue you mentioned regarding education, could you just explain to those who are not as familiar with Kosovo as you are why education was such an important factor for the Kosovo Albanian community.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There are two main issues here why education is more important there than in other parts of Europe. Firstly, because Kosova came out of the Second World War with a completely, almost completely illiterate population, and only because of education and a dynamic education system the society began to change dynamically and to create its modern institutions. So one of the reasons was heritage. The second reason is demographic. Kosova has the youngest population in Europe, and at that time in 1990, it was estimated that we had about 400.000 people involved in education, either pupils and students or teachers, because one-fifth or one-fourth of the population of Kosova at the time was young. In these demographic and heritage conditions that I described, the blow to education was much harder than it would have been for any other European country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to have Exhibit 696 in e-court. This is a 65 ter number 00696. This is a report of the secretary-general on the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. I take it, Your Honours, with the exhibit numbering we have in place, this would be Exhibit P1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There were a number of exhibits received yesterday. They have now been numbered by the Registry, so this will not be, I believe, be Exhibit P1 but will be some later number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P00265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. You will be surprised how the exhibit list grows. If you leave it alone in a corner that it just grows.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I have experienced that, Your Honour. Just for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention while we're doing that that following the raising of this matter before the Chamber, there were discussions yesterday, we are told, between the parties and the Registry; and it has been agreed to establish a normal numbering system for this trial, independent of any other, but with cross-reference where applicable to exhibit numbers in the Milutinovic et al trial. I'm grateful to the parties for having come to an agreed position over that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for my own clarity on how to proceed regarding exhibits, I'm going to be calling them with their 65 ter number, and I understand the Registry -- Registrar is going to be assigning the P numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. You refer to 65 ter number and then a new exhibit number will be given if the document is received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So could we have -- this exhibit is 0096.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the exhibit before you? Mr. Surroi --

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- do you have the exhibit before you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to turn to page 12 of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S and would like to zoom-in on paragraphs 47 and below under the heading "Kosovo." If we could zoom-in for the witness, so he's able to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, could you briefly comment on this section of this report.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At that time at the conference for peace in former Yugoslavia, a sub-group was set up of minorities in Kosova. That's how it was called. And a part of that special group in Kosova dealt with the issue of education. This happened as an initiative after the arrival of the Prime Minister Panic to Prishtina, his meetings with Dr. Rugova and the unexpected initiative to have talks on the normalisation of the issue of education. As you can see here, this began in 1992 with the establishment of the special group which would meet in Geneva. However, there were no results unfortunately from these meetings at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have Exhibit 00715 up on the screen. Could I also have the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just ask, are you meaning to do something about the report of the secretary-general as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was going to ask, Your Honour, do you want me to tender exhibits as I go along?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be more practical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think then I'm done with that exhibit. I seek to tender it into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is no opposition. The report of the secretary-general will be received as an exhibit. The Registry Officer will confirm the number for me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as previously assigned, P265 stands admitted and would be reflected in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the document that is currently on the screen, the "San Egidio Agreement on Education"?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the background of this document?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After the failure of the process in Geneva, which was evident in the report issued by the secretary-general, confidentially there were negotiations between Professor Agani and Serbian Ambassador in Vatican of Yugoslavia, that is, Maslovaric, on the normalisation of the education, Albanian education in Kosova. With "normalisation," they meant the return to the school facilities of the peoples without any obstruction and the initiation of a more normal process of education in Kosova. So that afterwards, new forms could be found for funding and other issues. This agreement was signed by Dr. Rugova and the Serbian president, and through this agreement there were three groups, three plus three were set up, three from Kosova, three from Serbia, which would deal with issues that were -- that had to be resolved. There were four years from Geneva process San Egidio Agreement, which was signed through the mediation of this charity organisation. And then from that time, two years passed without any implementation. They were still empty meetings of these mixed groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you're telling us -- I'm sorry, I had interpretation in my headphones. So this education agreement was signed by Dr. Rugova and Serbian President, who at the time was Mr. Milosevic; correct? But you're saying it was never implemented?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was not implemented in general. Only after two years this was stated by Professor Agani to Milosevic. When they met in 1998, even an issue which should not have been problematic, such as the return to school facilities, had been a problem for a long period. As far as I remember, on the basis of this accord, only the return of the Albanological Institute was implemented, only that point of the accord, and after some time or so the opening of the faculty of technology, which was destroyed until then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when did that happen, the return of the Albanological Institute?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This happened two years after the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So that would be sometime towards the summer of 1998? And when was the faculty of technology that you referred to opened or reopened?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it did not resume its work before the war because it was destroyed before the return. So it was required to make a lot of investments in order to rebuild the faculty or to repair it. So for that reason, as far as I remember, the European Union allocated some funds, which of course due to war were never, never put -- never actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How was the faculty destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The faculty was destroyed by the Serbian students of that time. They did not want that the faculty should be returned to the Albanians, so they organised big demonstrations, that is, the Serbian students. There was also, as far as I remember, police intervention at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, this agreement, the education agreement, established a mix group, a three-plus-three group was going to be set up to oversee the implementation. Could you tell us the composition of that mixed group? How was it supposed to be made up?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. From Kosova side there were three representatives. Unfortunately, one of them had an accident. He had a road accident which was not related to any political circumstances. The other members were also people who had dealt with the educational issues. One of them, if I remember well, had been involved also in the process of Geneva earlier, Mr. Abdyl Rama.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions on this document, and I seek to tender it into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number, Your Honours, 00715 will be assigned P00266.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, right after the agreement was concluded, were there demonstrations in Serbia concerning electoral practices?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There was a wave of demonstrations in Serbia, in general organised by the opposition. The opposition complained of lack of democracy, I mean the Serbian democracy, as well as for vote-rigging.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Vote-rigging by whom? Who was in power at the time? Vote-rigging by whom? You referred to vote-rigging.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It's clear this had to do with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, now, the next series of negotiations were carried out under the auspices of an institution called the Bertelsmann Scientific Foundation. Did you take part in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The Bertelsmann Foundation organised a track two, a negotiation called track two, which was intended to explore what could be the framework of addressing the issue of status of Kosova, how the status should be approached, what should be the measures of understanding and then in what framework, in what context, should the status of Kosova be examined. I took part in these negotiations from the outset.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 00712 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the document now before you? Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you comment on the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that the fundamental idea of all this dialogue was that the status of Kosova should be divided into several elements. The first element was the question of setting up measures of goodwill and normalisation of a life for citizens. It was very clear to all of us who took part in that dialogue that the status quo of Kosova would generate violence and armed conflict because it was a life without dignity which could not continue any longer. The second question which we tackled was that the status of Kosova could not be resolved immediately but through a process which would lead to the status -- to the settlement of the status. So there would be a need for negotiations after negotiations. And the third issue was that the status should be an open issue, not imposed, not restricted in the way it should have been resolved in the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this document that we have before us, this "Joint Recommendations on the Kosovo Conflict," were they the result of these negotiations that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. This was the outcome of the talks we had in Munich. They, in fact, started in Rhodes and then they continued in Munich and then they continued in Halki in Greece.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When were these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The first meeting actually began one day after the signing of the Agreement of San Egidio. The negotiations were in San Egidio were secret. There was no information about them. However, I know quite well that our talks began one day afterwards, because Mr. Agani came from that meeting in San Egidio directly to our talks. I'm talking about 2000 -- sorry, 1996. That is when the talks started, and then they finished in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately the month when these talks started in 1997?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It began in September 1996, and then they ended in September, in the same month, that is, in September 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your recollection, who else attended these talks?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From the Kosova side, from the outset, we had Mr. Agani, Professor Agani. In the end we had also Mr. Gazmend Pula.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who made up the Serbian delegation at these talks?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The Serbian delegation at the time included Mr. Predrag Simic, Mr. Radomir Tanic. These were the representatives from the Serbian side who took part in all these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were either these two persons you mentioned representatives from the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Simic was a part of a semi-official NGO. I don't think that he represented directly the government. He reflected to a large extent what the government thought. But Mr. Tanic, on the other hand, represented the New Democracy Party, which, through its chairman Mr. Mihalic, had access to government. This is what was told to us. That is, he had full access to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How seriously were these talks taken and what did they result?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: These talks or consultations or dialogue of non-governmental character had no obligatory character. They could not be considered as part of a serious state enterprise. Nevertheless, at the end of that process the foundations, Bertelsmann handed over this result to German Foreign Minister at the time, Mr. Kinkel. And as far as I know, then, Mr. Kinkel conveyed these documents and these ideas to Serbian President Milosevic when they met.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you see any changes or were any measures taken by the Serbian government as a result of these joint recommendations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Absolutely, no. At the time the conflict continued to escalate, the violence continued to escalate, and the war continued to escalate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you're referring to the conflict continuing to escalate, what exactly was happening in Kosovo? You're talking about the period when these talks ended, I presume, in September of 1997.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From 1997 onwards, that is, after these talks when we returned to Prishtina, we saw the intensification of police operations, especially in the region of Drenica. In November of that year, the UCK appeared in uniform. From that time, that is, following this emergence, until January 1998, we had the siege of Jashari family, for instance. So from day to day, from week to week, we had the intensification of the conflict. From a conflict of low intensity, it was becoming a conflict of higher intensity, of violence, until it reached the level of the war escalation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, before we move into 1998 I wanted to ask you about the last series of talks. Did you participate in a series of talks on a Project on Ethnic Relations in 1997? Can you tell us what that was about?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, the Project on Ethnic Relations had begun earlier. There was an effort again to reduce tensions, to set up a dialogue between Kosova and Serbia; and together with Professor Agani we had participated in a meeting which was organised in Belgrade one year before. Taking part in that meeting as representative of the Socialist Party, we met Mr. Percevic. At that meeting to which representatives of the government and opposition had been invited to meet representatives of Kosova belonging to the broad political spectrum of Kosova. So at that meeting, with the exception of Madam Pesic, we noticed that the situation in Serbia was tense. It was clear that the conflict could not be stopped, and it was clear to us that the situation would escalate toward the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to a first meeting organised in Belgrade. Was there a second meeting that later took place in New York, also in the framework of this Project on Ethnic Relations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The things which we described earlier took part in New York meeting. After the meeting in Belgrade we had the meeting in New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did these talks come to anything? Did they have any sort of result?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The outcome of them was again the conviction of everyone that if there were no changes, the conflict would escalate and there would be violence. It was in the interests of everyone at the time to try to avoid conflict, and this should be done through negotiations and through talks. However, this actually did not actually have any result.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender at this time Exhibit 00712, which is the joint recommendations that we were looking at earlier on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, in 1998 where were you living?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were you employed at the time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At the time, I was publisher of Koha Ditore newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this a newspaper that you had founded?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. I founded this daily newspaper following the publication of Koha magazine, which I also had founded earlier, and that magazine then was converted into this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When was this newspaper founded?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The newspaper was founded in 1997. The weekly magazine, on the other hand, was founded in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred earlier to the siege of the Jashari family. Could you first please tell us who was Adem Jashari?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Adem Jashari was an activist of his area, of his village, in the 1990s. He was afterwards one of the people who became active in an armed resistance. So we could say that he was one of the founders of the Kosova Liberation Army, both for the region where he lived but also for a broader area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where exactly did Adem Jashari live?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In the village Prekaz, in the region known as Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the siege of the Jashari compound that you referred to, when did it occur? When did it take place?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Initially we had some information about the siege, about possible operations in January 1998, but, in fact, the siege could have occurred later, at the end of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this an incident that your newspaper was covering?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. We had the permanent presence of journalists. They went to that region. They saw movement of UCK forces, and they also noticed an intensification of the activity of Serbian police forces in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened at the Jashari compound in March of that year, of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The family was encircled for several days in different forms. However, in March the family was actually placed under siege by armed vehicles and huge police forces. On the basis of the recount we had from our journalists on that day, as well as what we learned from two diplomatics who had come a little closer, as well as from what we learned from the BBC team which reported from our offices, so from all these sources we got information about the siege of the family. It was iron siege of Jashari family. They were asked to surrender themselves, but after their refusal to give up, the whole family was killed with the exception of those who could run away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who carried out this attack on the Jashari compound?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did your newspaper play any role with respect to the coverage in international that were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Our journalists went in most cases together with the foreign journalists because they had easier access; the foreign journalists had easier access to cross through, to pass through the roadblocks. Thanks to the agility of our journalists, we were able to have even photos. We were the first to have the photos of the killed family, which we distributed to all people who were interested in the photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now let's move to the G15. Could you tell us what was the G15?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: G15 was the negotiating group which was set up after the insistence of Ambassador Gelbard, US Ambassador Gelbard, who asked Kosova to prepare for negotiations. And these negotiations should take place with the participation of representatives from broad political spectrum in Kosova. I was one of the members of this group called G15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who else made up this group of the G15?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This group was chaired by President Rugova. It included other people, such as Mr. -- such Professor Agani, Mr. Bakalli, a broad spectrum of activists belonging to different political creeds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was US Diplomat Mr. Gelbard that you referred to earlier significant in persuading Mr. Rugova as to the attitude he should take in negotiations with Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Gelbard was able to convince or try to convince or help to have Mr. Rugova convinced in setting up a broader group of people. However, I believe that President Rugova was always ready for negotiations, so they came to terms together. They agreed that there should be negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the record, the last name of the US diplomat is Gelbard, spelled G-e-l-b-a-r-d.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, for practical reasons was this group the G15 reduced to the group called G5?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At the moment when we were to go to talk to President Milosevic, with the mediation of Ambassador Holbrooke, Mr. Holbrooke had mediated between Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Rugova then asked for the group to be reduced for practical reasons and that this group should be -- the new group should be composed of five people, including Mr. Rugova. This group will then go to talk to the Serbian president in Belgrade. Belonging to that group was Professor Agani, Mr. Bakalli, Mr. Nushi, and me; and, of course, the group was led by President Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You already told us who Mr. Agani and Rugova were. Who were Mr. Bakalli and Nushi that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Bakalli was one of the political leaders of the socialist times. He was a well-respected figures in Kosova. He had the respect of the whole political spectrum. Mr. Nushi was one of the founder of the human rights council in Prishtina. He was also a well-respected figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this group the G5 meet with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, the group met with the Serbian president in May 1998, on 15th of May. This was a meeting, as I said, arranged and mediated by US Ambassador Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the White Palace in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall what were the issues discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The meeting discussed a broad range of issues, starting from practical issues, such as the discussion on education; that was an issue raised by Professor Agani. But the meeting also discussed our demands related to the need to the interruption of the fighting and operations by the police. This demand was put forward by Mr. Bakalli on our behalf. The meeting also discussed the issue of Jashari. That issue was raised by me as an urgent issue which had to be resolved, that is, to see why had that massacre had occurred, and full light should be shed on what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what you told Mr. Milosevic about this massacre at the Jashari compound?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I raised the issue of the massacre of the Jashari family. Mr. Milosevic said that it was not possible, it was not possible that the police had killed civilians because only mad people would do such a thing. And I explained that from the information I had, it had -- that had happened, that innocent people had been killed. And anyway, in order to assert what had really happened, I demanded that a neutral forensic team come from Scandinavia so that they could really tell us what had happened with the Jashari family. And the answer given to me by President Milosevic was, "We'll see about that."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you take the impression based on this discussion you had with Milosevic that he had been briefed about the incident?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic spoke in so much detail about the incident so that I was convinced that either he was informed in detail just before the meeting took place or he had been in constant contact with the people who knew about the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was the issue of the status of Kosovo raised at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At the beginning President Rugova said that we want independence, but very soon the conversation diverted into another direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the ultimate goal of the G5 as far as Kosova's independence was concerned?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was clear, and we never concealed the fact that our objective was independence. It was also clear, I think, that in that meeting we did not go to that meeting to discuss status with Milosevic because that was the first meeting, and also we had other concerns in the meantime. So that meeting was just to break the ice, as it were, in order to jump-start a more complicated negotiating system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was the issue of education that we spoke about earlier discussed, addressed, at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Agani, in clear terms, raised the education issue. He said that there had been two years after the San Egidio Agreement and nothing had been implemented, although President Milosevic himself had signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Milosevic's reaction to your -- the issues you were raising, to your complaints?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: He tried to say that there was a nationalistic resistance in Serbia itself and all these issues would be solved when his act on education would be passed in the parliament of Kosova -- of Serbia. But my impression was that he was trying to link this issue with the issue of the purges he wanted to do in the University of Belgrade, where he wanted to purge the more democratic professors who were opposed to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At that time in May 1998 when this meeting took place, what was the situation on the ground with regard to confrontations between Serb forces and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In May there was already escalation, not only in Drenica but also in central Kosova. There was escalation of conflict and confrontations in the Dukagjini plain and in Decan. So starting from Peja, Gjakova, Decan, that was the area. And at that time there had begun movements of displaced people, of the first refugees of war, and especially in the Dukagjini plain, there was movement of people that would escalate into the first refugee crisis, the first refugees who would cross the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many refugees fled this fighting at the time, just a rough number.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We were concerned at the time for the fate of the refugees in the Decan area because there were about 5.000 of them, and the snow had not yet melted in the mountains. It was still May. And they had to cross the mountains and go over to Albania. They were not protected from weather or from anything else at the time. I don't know the exact number in May, but I know that between -- starting from the summer of that year, there were about 100.000 displaced people, refugees, in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any follow-up talks to this meeting that you had in May with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The agreement with Mr. Milosevic was that a week later, on the 22nd, we would meet the appointed Serb delegation in Prishtina and we would officially start the talks with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did this meeting take place a week later?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. The delegation came, and we held our meeting in the building of the League of Writers and the same building was used by the Democratic League of Kosova. The meeting was this delegation appointed by Belgrade. The talks attempted to identify the issues that we would discuss then and in the future. And with our insistence, at our insistence, although, in fact, we were insisting from the beginning that the talks would have to be mediated, Belgrade did not agree to the physical presence of a mediator in the talks. So we found a compromise issue. Ambassador Hill, the American Ambassador to Macedonia, was in the next room to where we were having the talks for consultation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour, that we're nearing the time for the break. I don't know if we should just interrupt here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that's a convenient time, we will certainly break now. I'm sure our witness will enjoy the opportunity to rest for a little while. We will resume when the tapes have been rewound in half an hour, at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, just to wrap up on the topic that we were discussing before the break, you were speaking about a meeting in Pristina in May 1998. Who attended that meeting from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From the Serbian side, the head of the delegation was Mr. Ratko Markovic, who was deputy prime minister. There was Mr. Stambuk, party of Milosevic's wife; Mr. Nikolic from the Serb radicals, and some other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did these talks result in anything? Did they accomplish anything?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, these talks failed because there was no framework as such that would create due process. There was no mediation, and in the end there was no agreement as to where these talks would take place. We insisted that the next meeting had to be held in Belgrade, while they insisted for the meeting to be held in Prishtina, and at the building of -- at the government building in Prishtina. They wanted to create the illusion that we were discussing an internal issue of Kosova in Prishtina, and there was no need for other parties to take place in it -- to take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any follow-up talks to this one?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. There were attempts on the part of Belgrade - I would call it a ridiculous attempt - to come to Prishtina. They were making public appeal for dialogue to Albanians in general, but they did not commit to a negotiating process. In the meantime Ambassador Hill was trying to keep the shuttle process alive by going to Belgrade and contacting the official representatives of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, moving to the period of the summer of 1999, you mentioned right before the break that there was an increase in refugee numbers, and I think you gave the number of 100.000 refugees, just that was your estimate. Could you tell us what was happening on the ground that caused this refugee crisis in the summer of 1999?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In the summer of 1998, there was a large-scale Serb offensive against the KLA forces but at the same time against the civilians, the Albanian citizens. At that time in July 1998, up until the end of September, more or less, there were fierce clashes on many fronts and this resulted into the displacement of the population. As far as I remember, before October 1998 the number of internally displaced persons was doubled. So by the end of September of that year we had a dramatic situation. Many people had no shelter above their heads and had created make-shift settlements, such as in Kishna Reka. People there lived under plastic sheets. At that time the movement of the Serbian police forces was directed not only towards central Kosova but also towards western Kosova, and part of the operations was -- part of the aim of those operations was to displace the population, the creation of a corridor of about 5 kilometres to the border with Albania, and the whole civilian population that was expelled from their homes was directed -- was sent in that direction. In central Kosova, in Rahovec, in Drenica, there was shelling which of course led to the fleeing of the civilian population. There were other activities, such as burning and looting of houses or private businesses and shops. For example, in Rahovec and in Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know which forces were involved in the large-scale offensive which took place in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From what I could see, I can say that there was a large presence of police forces from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were these police forces, units, that had previously been stationed in Kosovo, or were there also units brought in outside?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Before the July offensive or the summer offensive, there was an increase, extraordinary increase of the police forces that came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you become aware that there was an increase of police forces that came from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were reports from our journalists, but we also heard from people in general, the population, who saw the increase in numbers. Kosova is a very small place. It's 10.000 square kilometres. From one border to the other, you can go easily. So it's difficult to hide such a great or large-scale movement of military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to burning and looting of houses, businesses and private shops. How did you become aware that this was taking place?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After the summer offensive in 1998, maybe a week or ten days after Rahovec fell and the police forces entered Rahovec in large numbers, and this happened after KLA declared it liberated, Ambassador Hill and us, we were very concerned about the civilian situation in Rahovec; and we they went in the town of Rahovec, myself and Blerim Shala as well. But with us was also the human rights representative from Rahovec who showed us his burnt house. On the way to Rahovec, we and I could see personally Serb policemen who were looting the shops and properties in Malisheva. I saw the burnt houses, and on our way back, I saw a policeman who was going into a house and a few seconds later that house was on fire. Of course, he left the house before it was on fire. So all of these things were obvious to all of us in the convoy, that small convoy of cars. There were journalists with us as well. I can't remember now which agency they were with, but they were there and they reported on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to recognise this person that you saw going into the house which later was on fire? How were you able to recognise that that person was, in fact, a policeman?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: By his uniform, it was clear. It was a blue uniform, camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which uniforms were the soldiers, the Serbian soldiers or the VJ soldiers, wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The Serbian and the Yugoslav Army used olive-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know whether during the months that this offensive was carried out, whether there was any involvement or participation of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Later on, I can't give you the exact date, there was a unification of the command of police and military operations, but this was later on, much later on, maybe a few months before the NATO attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the population being expelled from their homes. Do you know who was carrying out the expulsions of the population?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From what I heard personally and from reports I had access to, it was the police. We saw this in Rahovec. I heard this in western Kosovo when we visited Junik. And I saw that with my own eyes after the shelling in Drenica. I visited there together with Ambassador Hill and Mr. Blerim Shala, and we were going to the KLA headquarters. We saw villagers who were leaving on their tractors, and very close to that village there was shelling from the positions of the police forces who were a few kilometres away. That was -- that was indiscriminate shelling against the village and the houses. They did not have a target as such. They were just shelling indiscriminately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is something you witnessed yourself, this shelling?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that myself with my own eyes. I could see the people leaving and the shelling taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this summer shelling came to an end?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The summer offensive ended in essence with the agreement Holbrooke-Milosevic. The American ambassador at the time started intensive negotiations because it was clear that the humanitarian crisis that was underway, caused by the summer offensive, was extraordinary and the refugees and the displaced -- internally displaced persons would be in danger. The winter was coming and when winter comes in -- and winter very often in Kosova comes as early as October. So the summer offensive ended when the international community intervened so that the military operation would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was end of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, did the situation in Kosovo on the ground change as a result of the conclusion of this agreement, the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement? And if yes, how did it change?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Some of the things changed. At the beginning, for example, there were no new developments. I mean there were no more -- no additional refugees leaving their homes. Some of the refugees who lived in very difficult circumstances, in plastic tents, as I mentioned in Kishna Reka, they started to go back to their homes or to their relatives. An additional effect was the arrival of the Verification Mission of Kosova. They started the confidence-building measures, and they started to report on the situation of -- in Kosova. In the meantime, both on the KLA side and the Serbian side, there was regrouping within the territory of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Following the period of the conclusion of this agreement, did the level of police forces and soldiers in Kosovo remain the same?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Part of the agreement was that some of the police and military forces would withdraw. There was an initial withdrawal of these forces. In fact, they had to demonstrate in front of the cameras that there was such a withdrawal, and this happened. And I think the situation was a little less tense, so from a very active conflict it descaled into a lower-scale conflict. But the constant presence and intimidation continued by the Serbian police forces towards the Albania civilian population. At that time, it was very difficult to circulate in Kosova because of the police check-points, where people were being ill-treated all the time. So it took them, for example, four hours to go through a check-point or to go through a road when, in fact, it would take only one hour normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the Rambouillet negotiations, Mr. Surroi. Did you participate in the Rambouillet negotiations of 1999?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in the Rambouillet negotiations, and I was one of the four members of the delegation who were, if I can call it, a leading position in the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when these negotiations took place, like, the period during which they took place?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The talks began in February 1999, and they were supposed to last for a week and then two weeks, but in fact they lasted for three weeks in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in addition to yourself, who else was attending these talks from the Kosovo Albanian side?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Of the four people I mentioned, there was Mr. Rugova, Mr. Hashim Thaci, and Mr. Qosja, who was chairman of a political party. There were representatives from the KLA, from the LDK, and, as I said, from the party of Mr. Qosja. The independents were Mr. Shala and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who made up the delegation from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The Serbian delegation was led -- or the negotiation process was led by Mr. Markovic, Mr. Stambuk, and sometimes Serb President Milutinovic, together with Mr. Sainovic. There were other members who were supposed to represent the ethnic communities in Kosova, but they did not represent anything in fact. But they were people who were very close to the Milosevic regime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But Milosevic himself did not take part in these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic did not take part in these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any international mediators present at these negotiations in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were three mediators who led the negotiations - Ambassador Hill from the United States of America, Mr. Petritsch representing the EU, and Mr. Mazowiecki representing the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And very briefly, can you tell us what was the purpose of the negotiations that took place in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The purpose of the Rambouillet negotiations was to create a transitional situation in which it would be possible for the refugees to return to their homes and to have some normality in life, but also the establishment of democratic institutions that would prepare Kosova to take an appropriate decision about its status within a three-year period. Of course there had to be no police and military presence in Kosova because they had exercised so much violence against the civilians at the time and the NATO forces would move in so that they could create a safe situation for an appropriate decision to be made with regard to the status of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your view was the Kosovo Albanian delegation serious in its attempts to reach a negotiated solution at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We were they determined to find a solution. It was very difficult. Our group was very heterogenous group, a mixed group. We didn't even know each other, some of us, but we arrived at -- we achieved a consensus in the negotiation process, a consensus that would create relations of partnership with the international community. We were determined to have an agreement that would lead to the establishment of democracy in Kosova and would create the possibility to have the right decision on the status of Kosova later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you perceive was the approach from the Serbian side regarding these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From the first week, or maybe I should say the first day, there was quite a great discrepancy between our attitude and theirs. I always thought that if we would really want to have negotiations, Mr. Milosevic had to take part in these negotiations. Well, he was absent, and the Serb delegation in the first week was completely different from ours. They did not deal with negotiations at all. They were just having fun there. And this created an imbalance in Rambouillet because we were very active in the negotiations while the Serbian part was extremely passive, and they were trying to procrastinate the process and even hinder it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did this negotiating process include or involve face-to-face negotiations between the two delegations, or were they shuttle negotiations?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The nature of the negotiations was that they would be held with the mediators. We were dealing with issues that were constitutional. We were discussing things about the future constitution of Kosova. So it was decided that we would communicate through the mediators and the legal experts so that we would come to the compilation of a document that would reflect the consensus. We did not shrink away from direct contact, face-to-face contact, but we were of the opinion that that would come after the negotiations through the mediators. So we had only one face-to-face meeting with the Serbian delegation, but that was only when Mrs. Albright was there. As I said, we were not shrinking away from that, but we wanted the document to be agreed upon first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did this document or this agreement that was available at Rambouillet for discussion, in essence, said what, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This document described Kosova in a transitional situation, what the arrangements would be in this transitional situation. This transitional situation implied the legal sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia until further decisions. It did not regulate on issues such as the customs or the establishment of a government and the parliament; a reduced presence of the police and the army, Serbian army forces in the territory of Kosova. And it described the obligation that within three years, in conformity with the will of the people, there would be a process that would decide on the permanent status of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And on the way to the formulation of this agreement, was the Serbian delegation, in your view, negotiating with real authority?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Because President Milosevic was not there, I believe the instructions were such that no negotiations -- nothing would be agreed upon that would make any concessions. This was clear when Mr. Sainovic flew urgently to Belgrade, although we had had a previous understanding with the mediators and Minister -- Secretary of State Cook and the others, that nobody would leave the council until the agreement had been reached. But when Mr. Sainovic went to Belgrade to meet Milosevic, then it was clear that the real decisions on the negotiations were taken by Milosevic and not the negotiators who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How did you find out that Mr. Sainovic had travelled to Belgrade to meet with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Ambassador Hill called me a few minutes before he was leaving himself together with Sainovic; and he said although it had been agreed earlier that nobody would leave, this was a special case, and he asked for the understanding of the Albanian delegation because it could be an opportunity for the negotiations to be pushed forward and maybe Milosevic would give his agreement for the negotiations to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at the return -- or when Mr. Sainovic returned from Belgrade, was there any change to the position of the Serbian delegation?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. The Belgrade delegation continued with their obstructing tactics, their procrastinating tactics, hoping that the differences we had within our delegation would lead to a lack of agreement within our delegation on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At the conclusion of these weeks at Rambouillet, did the Albanian delegation sign the document that was available for negotiation?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After a great many difficulties and accepting a formula that would lead to an agreement on the document but would need a process of consultation beforehand, I signed the document myself with a precondition that we had to consult our citizens first, and then we would go to Paris and then sign it on behalf of the citizens of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did the Serbian delegation sign the agreement that was available?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. The Serbian delegation did not sign. In the last hours of the conference, they offered to accept in principle part of the document and discuss the rest of it. But because we asked for extra consultation time, this consultation time was given to both parties so that they would reflect and with the hope that Belgrade would come closer to our position and sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While you were in -- at Rambouillet did you receive any information from your associates back in Kosovo, in Pristina, about what was happening there on the ground?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Part of our delegation, those representing the KLA, they had contacts in Kosova and they said that there was an escalation of the Serb police operations and the fightings.
