And the head of our dealings asked at the beginning of the meeting for a cease-fire, for a formal signing of a cease-fire; but this was not accepted by the Serbian party. And during that time, we had reports coming from a number of advisors we had in Prishtina and they also told us about the intensification of police activities in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did both delegations meet in Paris for further talks some weeks later?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: As we had promised, about two or three weeks later, we went to Paris, and the aim was to see how we could proceed further with the Serbian delegation. Our signing in Rambouillet was such that it regarded the document as completed in substance. And we thought that we need not go into the negotiation process again, but technical things could be amended while the Belgrade delegation wanted to start from scratch the whole negotiation process; and they wanted the whole thing to be based on the constitution of Kosova, everything that was decided on in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, in essence, what was the outcome of these Paris talks?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The outcome was that we officially accepted to sign the agreement, which was later called the Paris Agreement, while Belgrade refused it in its entirety. Our different approaches were clear to all the mediators, and not only the EU and the American representative, but also Mr. Mazowiecki, who was the Russian Federation representative, who saw the unwillingness of the Serbian party to take part in a negotiated agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the Serbian delegation present or attending those Paris talks was composed of the same persons that were -- had been attending the Rambouillet talks?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, but this time the delegation was headed by Serb President Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How many days or when did this -- these talks in Paris take place?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: They were three days, which were spent staying there. Then at the end of these three days we signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when these talks were held?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The third week of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Following these Paris talks, what was the reaction of the international mediators towards the Serbian delegation and the failure to reach a compromise regarding the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Upon our return to Prishtina, after some difficulties, before we entered Prishtina, Ambassador Hill, in Skopje, he informed us that he would make another effort together with Ambassador Holbrooke to try to talk with Milosevic so that they would try to persuade him to change his mind. So a final effort was made in which Ambassador Hill, Mr. Holbrooke, and the others went to meet Milosevic, to give him a last chance before the bombing would start, which had already been announced as a last resort in the absence of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This had been announced during the Paris talks or at Rambouillet? You were referring to the bombing as a last resort, had been announced.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Since the negotiating process, which interrupted temporarily the war, through Holbrooke-Milosevic agreements, NATO had installed its order which allowed the secretary-general to use force to prevent the Serbian police and some army forces. During the conference at Rambouillet, it was announced in different forms that if there was no agreement on the part of Serbian party, then this would imply that the bombing would start. So the absence of an agreement implied that the bombing would start. The goal of this action was to put an end to what was happening in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were these last final-effort negotiations that you referred to successful?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Obviously not. Milosevic refused. In the words of Mr. Holbrooke, Milosevic refused. Holbrooke had asked him was he aware of the consequences of his rejection, and Milosevic had replied that he was fully aware of the consequences of the rejection of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Following the failure to reach the negotiated solution, did NATO proceed to carry out a bombing campaign against Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. The bombardment started. They continued 78 days. During this complain NATO was successful in putting an end to one of the most barbarous campaign to the population in this part of Europe. More than 1 million Albanians had been displaced from their homes by the Serbian police and army forces. Thousands of people were killed. Even today more than 2.000 Albanians are reported as missing from that period. So these bombardments after 78 days led to the interruption on the basis of a UN Security Council Resolution 1244, which introduced the logic of Rambouillet Agreement, that is the creation of the conditions for the establishment of democratic institutions in Kosova and the creation of conditions for the settlement of the status of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to deal just very briefly with the period of the NATO bombardment. Do you recall when it started, when NATO started its bombing campaign?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: On 24th of March, after 8.00 in the evening, 8.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where were you when the NATO bombing campaign started?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I was in the house of my mother. I was together with my mother and father.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this was in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the Kosovo Albanian population to the start of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that there was a mixed feeling, joy and fear; joy because in the end, there was this major military force which would put a stop to the Serbian forces; fear because the war was assuming greater dimensions and people who had been suffering so much under police -- Serbian police action, under Serbian political action and under what was for a long time a fascist rule, so people feared punishment, the civilian population could suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the Serb forces that were on the ground deployed in Kosovo once the NATO bombing campaign started?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: From the first night, the punishment got started. In the morning when I woke up after a noisy and busy night with contacts with people, the first thing we learned in the morning was that one street of Prishtina, one quarter, one district of Prishtina was in flames. The streets were filled with armed Serbian soldiers and policemen. On the 25th, in the morning, I was called by the -- I was called by a friend of a lawyer, who was also my friend, and he told me that Bajram and his two sons, Kastriot and Kushtrim had been taken away by the Serbian police. They were taken away sometime during the evening, and he told me he was trying to learn from the police. He called me from somewhere close to the police station on his mobile, and he told me that he was at the police -- near the police station in order to learn about what was -- what has happened with these three people. This news was later confirmed by the wife of Bajram. I called her, and she also confirmed to me that the police had been in their house and had taken Bajram and his two sons. She had pleaded with the police that they should not take at least the youngest son, who was 17 years old, but the police did not listen to her. Later we learned that somewhere near Prishtina, near a pump, they had been executed. Then we learned about the remains of the persons who were executed, where they were located, later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned a person by the name of Bajram. Could you explain who he was?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Bajram Kelmendi was one of the most renowned lawyers. He was a legal expert in Kosova. He was one of the founders of the Kosova Council for the Protection of Human Rights in Kosova. He was a defender of many human rights cases. A few days before the bombardment started, three days before the bombardment, he had been also the counsel of the last case. The last case had to do with Koha Ditore, which had been persecuted by the regime due to the publication of a report. The trial had taken place on Sunday, which was extraordinary. It is extraordinary for any country in the world. And Bajram had been present in that session. That was the last day on which I saw Mr. Kelmendi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other prominent figures like Mr. Kelmendi who suffered once the NATO bombing began?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Another activist Mr. Hajrizi was killed that night in Prishtina. During the first week, as we learned, many well-known people in Gjakova were killed, where the persecution was even greater.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to these two prominent persons being killed by police. What was the situation of just a regular citizen, the Kosovo -- a regular Kosovo Albanian living in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In the first days, there was a nervous and fearful situation among the citizens of Prishtina, what had gone earlier in other towns like Peja or Gjakova, where people came out of the houses only to meet their elementary needs, to buy bread or get supplies, food, and then stood all the time within their homes. This now had become also the way of life in Prishtina. People went out very early from the houses. They just met their elementary needs, and then they confined themselves in their homes, following the situation. This continued in the first weeks. Then at the end of the first week the massive expulsion of the citizens from some parts of Prishtina began. The expulsion was exacted by the Serbian police forces, asking people to leave Prishtina and accompanying them, escorting them up to the railway station in Prishtina, in Fushe Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you were talking about the massive expulsion of citizens from part of Prishtina, were any particular ethnic groups forced to leave, or was this targeted towards any particular ethnic group, these expulsions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: All were Albanians. All who were expelled were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you become aware that this was happening, that these expulsions were taking place?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In one part of the district where I lived, I could see clearly the streets and that day, on 1st of April, if I'm not mistaken, a very big wave, a river of people got under way, escorted by the Serbian police. These people were heading towards Fushe Kosova. These were people who were clearly evicted from their homes because they carried with them only some plastic bags and some bread with them and some immediate things. So they were not given time to collect more things; they were just expelled from their homes promptly. This also continued to happen the next day. The next day actually I went into the house of a friend of mine, a childhood friend, and there I saw that the house was empty. All the family members had been expelled. However, I saw in the stove still dessert which had been baked by the housewife. It was still warm. And I could see also the teapot, with the tea boiling on the stove. So that was an indication to me that these people were expelled within five minutes. They were not given time even to take the dessert out of the stove or to stop things happening in the kitchen until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were any members of your family affected by these expulsions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: My sister Flaka at that moment she was compelled to stay with some friends, that is, with people with whom she had worked, as well as with some unknown people in an apartment which was located in another part of Prishtina. So she was forced on 1st of April to get out of that apartment, by force, and join the convoy with other citizens toward Fushe Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say the persons, the citizens of Pristina, were being exported to the train station. What was happening or what took place once these persons arrived at the train station in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Before they went out into the street, I saw this: On 2nd of April, when I came out and I had to go somewhere, so I saw that people were stripped of their personal documents. I saw with my own eyes a big group, a big mass of identity cards which had been piled. These documents were taken from the people and then the people were ordered to move towards Kosova Polje where they were ordered to get into the train and then travel up to the border with Macedonia. They would stop at Hani i Elezit, and then from Hani i Elezit, they would walk along the railway line up to the border with Macedonia where they would become refugees at the moment when the Macedonian authorities would receive them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the significance of these refugees being stripped of their personal documents before being taken to the train station?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The goal was to deprive them of their institutional and administrative identity, so they would not come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, based on what you were able to witness during those first -- that first week in Pristina and the contacts you had with people, did you get the impression that any of these persons who were heading to the train station Pristina were leaving because they were afraid of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, on the contrary. I passed the whole period of bombardments in Prishtina. The worst period for us who were there was the period when there was no bombardment because when there was no bombardment, there was more intense movement of Serbian police forces in Kosova. In the days when there was more intensive bombardment, there was a paralysis of the movement of the Serbian police forces in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not sure you answered my question. I was asking specifically of the motive the persons had for leaving. Did you get the impression that they were leaving because they were afraid of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Absolutely not. They were frightened directly from the order that they should leave their homes. They were also frightened from the persecution exercised on them by the police forces whenever they were in the districts, houses, or in their villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mentioned you were out on the street and saw this pile of documents. Were you able to observe any destruction to homes or to buildings in the times that you were able to leave the place where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In Prishtina there was not much destruction. There, what happened was stealing, and there were also acts of burning down. But compared to other parts of Kosova, in Prishtina there was no such destruction. In the streets about which you were asking, what was symbolic of what was happening was the fact that this street is named the Church Street because there's an orthodox church in the vicinity of the streets, and the residents of the houses in the streets had put the icons in the windows. So those houses which had the icons in the windows were intact. I saw one such house which did not have such an icon on its window, and that house had been destroyed. It had been stolen. It had been looted, and then I saw also signs of destruction of that particular house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that houses that had orthodox icons on the windows were not destroyed, were not touched.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. They were completely intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would it be fair to understand that these were houses that belonged to the Serb population of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What about the houses belonging to the Kosovo Albanian population of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Those houses had suffered looting. I saw in the house of family Bilishti, where I -- I told you that I was there on the 1st of April. On the 2nd of April, in that house, the police had entered, had searched the house, the shelves, and they had taken away valuable things. However, during those days I don't think they had much time to do that. You should remember that the number of people leaving their places was so big that the police had not much time to go after looting or stealing. So what was happening was simply a momentous destruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have an idea of approximately how many people were expelled from their homes during that first week following the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that you remained in Pristina throughout the NATO bombing. Were there other similar waves of expulsions that occurred later on in the weeks or months following?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There was an effort to make a registration of the population. That effort obliged all the Albanian inhabitants to register their location. However, what happened afterwards was that the massive -- that the waves of expulsions were not as massive as before. So what I want to say is that the waves of people leaving their homes were not as huge, as big, as before. After the scenes which we saw with the train, then what happened afterwards were to a lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this conflict in 1998 came to an end?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, in 1999.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: On 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what happened at the conclusion of -- in 12th of June, at the conclusion of [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: On 12th of June, we saw the British soldiers entering Kosova. On 11th of June, the Russian forces had come, but this did not stop the conflict. There had still been acts of destruction and firing in Prishtina. So on 12th of June, the British forces of NATO entered Prishtina and that was then that we learned that the war had come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to ask you just one last question on an unrelated topic and this has to do with an expression that we will hear often in the course of this trial. This is the expression of "Siptar." And I wanted to know, from your point of view as a Kosovo Albanian, what do you understand the word "Siptar" to mean?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Siptar is the name we use for calling ourselves. However, after the Second World War and after Kosova remained in Yugoslavia, particularly during the 1950s, the word "Siptar" used in Serbian language had assumed a negative connotation. From a political point of view, in Serbian, Siptar means Albanian, but those who Serbs who used the word Siptar could have took cultural context. The first goal was to make a distinction between Albanians of Albania and Albanians of Kosova or Yugoslavia. Therefore, many Serbian-speaking people used "Albanac" for Albanians of Albania and Siptar for Albanians of Yugoslavia. But the word "Siptar" had also a negative cultural connotation, in the articulation and description of someone who dealt with physical jobs, so it referred to a citizen of a second rank. So in Belgrade certain sections used the word "Siptar" by referring, for example, to people who were needed to cut wood or people who would be used to transport coal. Like, they didn't say for example, Bring the worker here to transport wood, but bring the Siptar here to transport wood. So in cultures where there is under-evaluation of other ethnicities, you see the same thing. In California, referring to such people, for example, they don't say, for example, Go and get a worker, but go and get a Mexican, for example, as the person who would come and mow the grass.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if the term is used by someone from Serbian ethnicity, would you understand it to be used in a derogatory term -- in a derogatory way?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I believe that this was the sense for which this word is used, yes, in the negative sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Kravetz. I see the time and it seems that this would be a sensible time to have our second break and to allow, then, the cross-examination to commence after the break. So we will break now to resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, the time has come for you to commence cross-examination. As we are just feeling our way into the trial, could I say a few things relating to cross-examination which will apply in due course equally to the Prosecution. We are, as a Chamber, concerned to allow a fair and proper airing of the issues. For that reason we prefer not to fix absolute times for examination or cross-examination, although in some other Chambers there is a practice to set fixed times and counsel must keep within them. While we avoid fixing fixed times, you will appreciate that we must be constantly concerned about the time of the progress of the trial. This could be an extremely long trial unless everybody is very disciplined about time and that means also that questions by counsel need to be very disciplined so that they are important and relevant, and we don't lose time dealing with issues that don't really matter in the end. As long as counsel are dealing with relevant and important issues, this Chamber is unlikely to interfere in the progress of an examination or cross-examination. But if it appears that counsel is dealing with issues that are not so important, we certainly may interfere to urge counsel to move on. We will also be keeping an eye on the total time spent with a witness out of concern that this trial will finish as soon as it properly can, so that if you could be aware of that. And if we think too much time is being spent, we will indicate that as well. If things do not go responsibly and effectively, you will appreciate we may have to impose fixed times. But we would prefer to avoid that to give counsel as much opportunity as possible to deal with what they consider to be important issues. So with that in mind, we'd be grateful if you could deal with the important issues from your client's point of view. I would mention that we understand the witness is concerned himself with his timetable and other commitments. Unfortunately, the Chamber would see little prospect of the witness being able to leave today. I mean, we have only one further hour before we must finish because we have only half a day use of this courtroom, and that would mean that it is inevitable, we fear, that the witness's evidence will continue beyond today. Because there is no courtroom available, we do not sit tomorrow, and we sit again on Friday. There would be, though, a good expectation that the witness will finish his evidence in the course of Friday's hearing. I'm sorry if that causes difficulty with your plans, but you will understand that your evidence is significant in this trial; and from the Chamber's point of view, it wants to hear your evidence, and it wants to hear the issues you've raised properly explored not only by the Prosecution but also by the Defence, so that in the end, we can come as best we can to a proper decision. Your cooperation is appreciated in that. Sir, if you would like to commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as the Defence counsel, I must first apologise because perhaps at the beginning of the trial I will have some problems because the legal system where I practice does not really know cross-examination. It's not the usual practice, to cross-examine witnesses that were called by the Prosecution. But I do believe that this will change as this trial progresses

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to greet Mr. Surroi, our witness, and to say that I'm hear representing Vlastimir Djordjevic, who is not related to me although we share the same surname. I'm representing him but it's a very frequent name in Serbia. I have been an attorney for a long time, mostly dealing with criminal cases. I am also the vice-president of the bar association, and I am quite well-known in Belgrade, but let me not waste our time with it. Let us move on to the questions. In accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I am entitled to first explore the issues that arise from the examination-in-chief and then I will proceed to explore some other relevant issues, relevant for the defence of my client. First of all, I understand that this witness has presented us with a historical context of the events, and this witness also provided some material evidence about the actual context of the events, but I will now first ask you some questions about the period from 1974, which was when the constitution was adopted granting Kosovo a broad autonomy in relation to the 1989 constitution, which, as you say, reduced the autonomy of Kosovo, of its assembly, and transferring most of the powers again back to Serbia. My first question to you, this is what I'm really interested in, is if you're involved in politics. And if yes, since whether?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I am involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you been involved in politics? This is my second question, the second part of my question.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I wanted to know whether you're asking me --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you having difficulties? You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not receiving interpretation. I'm not receiving interpretation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know whether I am a professional politician or do I participate in politics as an activist?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question, first of all, is whether you are involved in politics. You said that you were. Being a professional politician, well, that was not my question because if we were now to go into a debate about what being a politician or being involved in politics entails, we would waste a lot of time. I know that you were a member of the assembly, a representative in the assembly. I know that you were involved in politics. But I want you to tell the Chamber all that. I know that you were a member of the Democratic Initiative, which was active in our former state, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Okay. So you told me that you were involved in politics, but now I want to know, since when have you been involved in politics? Could you please tell us the date?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In an organised form I have been involved since 1989, from the founding of the first democratic organisation Ujdi and with my role in the organisation of the independent trade unions in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as regards the assembly, the 1989 assembly - my colleague has dealt with that issue - I wanted to ask you whether you were a member of that assembly.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's another thing that I'm interested in. Do you know what the ethnic composition that was of the Kosova Assembly, the 1989 assembly? Percentages. Give us an approximation.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was the competition of the assembly such that the representatives of Albanian ethnic background were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: You know that in accordance with the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the 1974 constitution, the constitution was the same. The only thing that differed was that instead of Kosovo, it said the Socialist Autonomous Province of Vojvodina, and there were more official languages in use in Vojvodina than there were in Kosovo. What I'm interested in is relates to the existence of this other province. Do you know what happened in the assembly of the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina at the very same time when the events unfolded with the Kosovo Autonomous Province Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I know what occurred there, but I don't see any relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As a professional, as an attorney, I'm not talking about legality, I'm talking about legitimacy. And this is why I would like to remind you that at that time there was the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under which there existed two autonomous provinces; and it is relevant because at that time you must know that there were two autonomous provinces - the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina and the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. The latter had the assembly that you were telling us about. Now I want to tell you, I want to ask you, whether it is true that at that time, 1989, the constitution of the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina was changed in the same way in which the constitution of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija was changed? In other words, that power was devolved to the assembly to the Republic of Serbia; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Differently from the Vojvodina Assembly, the Kosova Assembly was surrounded with APCs and uniformed and armed police, with long arms. And differently from the Assembly of Vojvodina, in the Assembly of Kosova, people who voted there, some of them were people who were not members of the parliament. One of them, for example, was the director of the prison service and he -- his name was Mehmet Ajeti, and there is a picture of him voting there in the parliament. He was not a member of parliament; he was a lackey of Milosevic. And there were other people like him as well who were there illegitimately and who voted illegitimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the presence of police and combat vehicles. Could you please explain that. Clarify what kind of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: They were APCs - that's what they're called in English - armoured vehicles of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone threaten the deputies in the assembly, force them to vote this way or another, or do you consider that the very presence of the police around the assembly made the assembly act in the way that it actually did?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were direct threats as well. One of the lawyers, Mr. Syla Bukovci was kidnapped by the Serbian police. He was taken by helicopter to an unknown location, according to what he told his family, and he was threatened because of this issue, the constitutional changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member or a deputy in the assembly? Did he vote there?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: He was member of the Committee for Constitutional Changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did he vote at the assembly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it because he was not actually the deputy in the assembly or because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please wait for the end of the interpretation into English of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... describing it here, and I'm also relaying to you the words of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that the witness was able to hear the interpreter's remark because he does not have his earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were asked if you could, Mr. Surroi, to wait until you hear the translation of the question finish before you answer because you're tending to start to answer before the translation is completed, and the interpreters are not able then to deal both with your answer and the finishing of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So let me go back to the question that relates to this lawyer. His name now escapes me. Was he a deputy in the assembly or was he merely the chairman of the commission for the constitutional changes, or a member thereof? Could you please just clarify that very briefly and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I can't remember whether he was a member of the assembly or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then I won't be asking you any more questions about that. As regards the 1989 assembly, could you explain to me how did it come to pass that the assembly voted in favour of, let's say, Serbia and, according to you, to the detriment of the Albanian nation in Kosovo, if we take into account the fact that the majority of deputies at that time were of Albanian ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, there was pressure, and there was an extraordinary situation. I don't think that assemblies should take decisions when they are surrounded by military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are there any documents about the fact that the assembly was surrounded by armoured vehicles? Are there any photographs from that period? Because you have to admit -- and I have to tell you that I'm not aware of it and that is why I'm asking you this. Is there any evidence - photographs, articles published by international media - that Serbia put tanks around the assembly while the assembly was taking a vote?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Well, if you look for them, I think you can find them. I'm speaking here about things that I have seen with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I asked you. I have looked for that, and I haven't been able to find any, but thank you for your answer. In the period between 1974 and 1989, do you know that there were any demonstrations in Kosovo? And if you know that, do you know what motivated the protestors, what reasons were behind them, and what was the outcome of the demonstrations, as I call them? You keep talking about the Serbian police, and we're talking about the period between 1974 and 1989. Was there a presence of the federal police, the confederal police, because Yugoslavia was a federal state; a federal police force that took part in suppressing the unrest in Kosovo and Metohija? And do you know that, for instance, when it comes to the Trepca mine, that it was the federal police force that intervened there. It included police officers of Albanian ethnic background, Serbs, Slovenes, Bosniaks, as we call them now - there was a different term used then - and Macedonia. So that's my question. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were many questions there and I'll try to be brief in my answer. The first one was about the administration -- correction: Were there any demonstrations? Yes, there were, in 1981 and later as well. In those demonstrations, the people were demanding the status of autonomy within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and those movements or demonstrations were suppressed with excessive use of force by the Yugoslav bodies. In the later demonstrations, starting from 1988, 1989, 1990, in the beginning in 1988, 1999, the demands were for the protection of the autonomy of Kosova and to save it, as it were, from the Serbian Anschluss and subordination. And these demonstrations were quelled and suppressed by the Serbian police, which had come to Kosova. With regard to Trepca, I think there were other units from the Yugoslav federation as well there, but if I remember correctly, Slovenia and Croatia had withdrawn their units. In the end Macedonia, did the same. Their units were stationed in Ferizaj. This happened in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not agree with you when you say that Slovenia, Croatia, and Macedonia pulled out their units, but let us not go into that. Let me move on to the next question. I think it merits an answer because it has to do with logic. The 1974 constitution envisaged the broadest autonomy for the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija, so at that time the people living there was governed by a constitution that enabled it within the framework of the Socialist Federal Yugoslavia to have the broadest possible autonomy, to have its own courts, education system, and so on. I fail to understand what the demands were that were put forward at the demonstrations. So you're talking about 1981, and then you talk about 1983, and then you go on to 1989. So what the demands -- what were the demands? Were those the demands of the people living in that area which logically then lead to the quashing of all of those rights that they enjoyed in 1989? So if they had those rights according to the 1974 constitution, what more did they ask for in 1981? Because you keep talking about the autonomy. Okay, yeah, autonomy existed under the 1974 constitution. You even used the American term "veto," that Kosovo had the right to veto in the national assembly. But if you're talking about autonomy and the 1974 constitution, if you're saying that the autonomy was at such a level that, for all intents and purposes, in 1989 it happened that all the rights were taken away, that everything was devolved to the Republic of Serbia - education, courts, and so on - so why were there those demonstrations in 1981 and then later? I will not now go into what happened and what the outcome was of all that. We'll deal with that later. But can you please find me a logical explanation? Why demonstration if we have a constitution that is in force which accords full autonomy to the people in Kosovo, and its organs, all of them, all the bodies?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The response is both simple and complicated. At the same time, simple, if you refer to logic. The logic is based on human rights and the right of the people to articulate their demands. Human history has lots of examples of people demanding more and more, demand more and more progress. The logic you refer to, the logic of suspension is anti-democratic logic. It's irrelevant as what you describe as positive or not positive. Every citizen has a right to express his desire to demand his or her rights. It's not the right of the people to act against the desire expressed by people peacefully, by resorting to violent means. In 1981 and 1982 people were beaten up because they expressed political demand. In 1988 and 1989, 1990, people were beaten up and killed because they used other forms of demanding political rights. In both cases, the demand is not important. The important thing is to see what is the reaction of the regime to the demand, to see the totalitarian regime, the nature of this regime. This regime resorted to violence instead of dialogue, which should be the method used in a democratic, free society.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will admit that in terms of modern history we have to make a distinction between democracy and anarchy, anarchy and totalitarianism, and dictatorship. When it protects its sovereignty, every state has to take measures in order to protect the constitutional order. That is why I don't agree with you. Because what would we do, then, if we were to go into the examples of other peoples who also have a wish for a greater autonomy, a state of their own; say the Basque in the Spanish, and then the Irish, and the Flemish, and the Walloons so on and so forth. History showed that both solutions have their positive and negative sides. However, I will just agree with you on one thing, that dialogue as a method of changing things is indispensable, rather than violence. Now I'm going to move on to my next set of questions. We heard from you, although I must say we weren't exactly happen to hear that, that the forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia acted in the territory of Kosovo, protecting the constitutional order while Marsal Tito was still alive, and then after that things were changed. Of course ultimately it ended with the Serbian forces, now, whether it was the police or the army, that is something we're going to establish during the course of these proceedings, and who played what role in that context. However, if we talk about relationships in Kosovo, I'm not going to talk about relations between other ethnic groups and Albanians, Siptars, and then -- actually, when I say "Siptar," Mr. Surroi, I say that with the utmost respect, because I know that you yourselves call yourselves that. I know that Albania is called Siptaria, so I really don't see anything derogatory about that. Now, of course, it depends on one's point of view. What is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if my learned colleague from the Defence could be asked to state a question to the witness. I see that he's making statements on the record, and I don't see the question being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're quite right, Ms. Kravetz, but at this stage the Chamber is allowing Mr. Djordjevic to shape his cross-examination as he feels. But you'll appreciate that at the moment often you're really entering into a debate with the witness rather than asking a question and getting an answer, and we expect that you'll gradually move to question-and-answer form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is precisely because of the context of the witness's statement that I am doing this. As for the objection raised by the Prosecutor, I certainly accept that, but I kindly ask that you do not interrupt me. I did not interrupt you during your direct examination. I precisely wanted to discuss what it was that you raised, Ms. Kravetz, as a question. On the basis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we have to deal with the questions that you raised during the direct examination and the Defence has the definite right to do that. And I do admit that I have been speaking at quite a length.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now the question: The demonstrations that took place in Kosovo, in a way, were they such that they caused material damage, injuries to people, not by the police but by other rioters; also the destruction of property, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: If I could respond to both questions, Mr. Djordjevic. There are Serbs who describe themselves as Shkji in Kosova, but when an Albanian calls the other Shkji, then this word carries a cultural background, an emotional connotation. Therefore, I'm not calling you or your compatriots as Shkji. You should also respect your linguistic context. I will also respect my linguistic context. During the demonstrations of 1981 and 1982, there might have been some glasses broken or there might have been some damage to some property, but all of this is irrelevant if you compare it to the damage caused to human life. A person who is killed for raising a political demand cannot be justified by comparing it with another act of violence. The violence you are talking about in 1981, 1982, 1988, 1989, was not violence exercised by the demonstrators. This is the logic of the totalitarian regime. This was violence exercised by the regime against the people. I saw this violence with my own eyes when it was exercised. I saw how the police officers beat up innocent citizens who had one political desire, one political idea, they wanted to give vent to by using peaceful means. I was myself beaten up by the Serbian police, and this happened while I was manifesting my desire for peace in Kosova against war, against violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I certainly regret that, Mr. Surroi, if that happened to you, just like any normal person would do. I would be interested in the following: In the context of this policy you mentioned that people were laid off, after 1980, Albanians who didn't want to sign statements of loyalty; and in that context many of them remained jobless and you said that policemen were also dismissed from the police force, quite a few of them, and you also said that Albanians who had socially owned apartments had their apartments taken away from them. I would like to move on to the next question. Do you know that Albanians who were dismissed were involved in proceedings before courts of associated labour as they were known at the time in the places where they lived and worked while resorting to the right that everyone had at the time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: A small number of people did this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the outcome was of such proceedings? Because I personally represented some Albanians before courts of associated labour precisely at that time.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I am not aware of many cases, but I believe one or two have won.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All of those who brought a case before the court won, but not everyone resorted to the civic rights that they had at the time, that is to say, the right they had to take their cases to a court. That goes for a policeman as well; you will agree with me on that. As for apartments, I do apologise, I do not know of a single case - sorry, perhaps you do, but if you do, please tell us - would you please tell me of a single case of an Albanian who had his apartment taken away from him, any Albanian who lawfully got an apartment from the company where he worked? It would be very hard for this Trial Chamber to understand this, but we, from that part of the world, know that social ownership is a type of ownership in property that no one can understand who's not from that part of the world. It is not public property, it is not state property, so no one knows of this except from us who are from that part of the world. So do you know of a single case of an Albanian who had been given a socially-owned apartment, had it taken away from him?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were some cases like this. I cannot tell you now exactly how many. As I said in my statement in the questions put forward by the Prosecutor, this was a limited number of people. This was not a massive phenomenon. A massive phenomenon was the dismissal of people from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: You spoke about refugees - we are moving on now to 1998 - and you first mentioned the figure of about 5.000 persons who, before this summer offensive as you called it, left their apartments and so on and so forth. First of all, how did you come up with this figure, 5.000? How did you get that figure? That was my first question.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In May, I think, 1998 we had a meeting with Ambassador Hill. It took place on Saturday and Sunday. We had at this meeting reports about the refugees. This report came from different sources, from newspapers as well as from human rights activists. We asked in the presence of Ambassador Hill that the question of refugees from Decan area should be addressed, because we had a report of the humanitarian crisis. As I mentioned earlier, the snow had not melted away yet and people were not able to cross the border into Albania. We asked for the UNHCR office; however, that office had evacuated its staff from Belgrade. We contacted with Madam Ogata, who at that time was the high commissioner for refugees. In our presence, the number of 5.000 people was confirmed. This was the number of people who were in the mountains of Decan at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was present at that meeting with Ambassador Hill?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were some members of the negotiating team, Mr. Shala, it was me, and there were also some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That means that that was a meeting between Ambassador Hill and the representatives of the Albanian people in Kosovo; right? It was not a meeting with the Serb side as well. Were there any Serbs present?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This was a meeting between our negotiating team and Ambassador Hill. After this meeting, Ambassador Hill went to Belgrade to meet with the Serbian authorities there. We explicitly asked that the issue of refugees should be raised with the Serbian side so that these people were at least provided with safe get-away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what did that meeting with Ambassador Hill result in?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Madam Ogata personally took up the issue of refugees. The negotiating team referred for admission in Kosova. As far as I know, the issue of refugees was raised with representatives of Serbian government. I'm not exactly aware who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, I just wanted to get a response as to how the issue of these 5.000 refugees was resolved. Did they all go back to Decani? Were they all Albanians, or were they people who left that area that you referred to, while they had different ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: They were all Albanians and all ended up as refugees. In Albania, there were Kosovo Albanians. The UNHCR tried to create -- to provide them with basic conditions on the other side of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this problem, the problem of refugees, you mentioned that there was excessive use of force by the state organs, specifically the police; and that that was a result of the fact that these refugees actually started moving towards Albania; and that's how the problem came up. Do you know why the Serb police engaged in these activities that resulted in this number of refugees of Albanian ethnic background only? Do you know what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I could assume some reasons. However, I think it's totally irrelevant for me to provide you explanations why such refugees emerged. For me it's important to say that these were 5.000 people, refugees, who were expelled from their homes. What was in the hearts of the policemen, what was in the hearts and minds of the officials, then this is something which probably you might deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, I am not going to enter a polemic in terms of what you said now, the last thing you said, and I'm not going to be offended in any way. I'm just going to say that the police is not there to carry something in their hearts; they are a state organ that is supposed to discharge its duties. In Pristina, the capital of the Serbian Autonomous Province of Kosovo, was totally blocked. The road from Pristina to Pec, you could not take that road because there was a big trench dug in the middle of the road with machine-gun nests that had been dug by the KLA. So if you wanted to go from Pristina to Pec, you had to leave your country, you had to go to Montenegro, and then via Kula to go down to Pec; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: As I said, it's totally irrelevant for me. I am not going into details whether there had been fighting between UCK and Serbian forces. For me it is -- what was relevant was that the Serbian police were persecuting the civilians, and this is on what the talks focused, that is, how conditions could be created so that the civilians could be safe. As far as the war is concerned, it's another issue. The issue of the protection of human rights is quite another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is not a humanitarian organisation, it's a court of law, we are interested in all the relevant circumstances. I will understand this as your evasion of giving a direct answer to my question. Anyway, there is a way of establishing what the situation was. The police took all measures at the time so that the inhabitants of the country could move about freely, irrespective of the machine-gun nests, and things like that. Of course, everyone has to be concerned about a humanitarian catastrophe, but we always have to go into the context of everything that was going on. My next question takes us back to the constitution of 1989. Mr. Surroi, tell me, this constitution, did it abolish bilingualism in Kosovo or not?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Instead of equality of languages, this constitution introduced the supremacy of the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And was the official use of the Albanian language prohibited?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, but in practice this supremacy led to the establishment of a distance which was -- which cannot be imagined now. If I could give you one simple example, the Serbian regime, after taking over Prishtina, later on television it allowed the broadcasting of the Albanian language programme; so there was Albanian language programme broadcast both by television and radio. But there were more Albanian language programmes in Moscow radio, Helsinki radio, than in Prishtina radio. If you have 90 percent of the population being Albanian, this was not a normal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question: In schools was bilingualism abolished? Were there still classes in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In the elementary schools there was bilingualism, that is, parallel classes in Albanian and Serbo-Croatian. However, the schools were physically separated by walls. The pupils who were taught in Serbian language had state funding, while the children who attended Albanian language classes had funding from parallel structures or bodies. For example, I could give you -- I could bring you my own example. When my daughter went to the first grade, she went to the same building where there were Serbian children as well. However, the school was separated by a wall, and the Serbian children had heating in the classes, the children in the Albanian-portion of the same building had no heating during winter and were very cold. In the secondary schools, all the students in the building in Prishtina were removed from that building, those who attended the Albanian language classes and were forced to enter into buildings run -- ran by parallel bodies. The same happened with Prishtina University. If the judicial system had maintained the bilingual system, as you said, then there would have been no need for the negotiating process, such as San Egidio or Rambouillet, to bring the Albanians back to a normal education system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now you've totally confused me, Mr. Surroi. You are talking about a parallel system, and you're talking about a schooling system, or, rather, the schooling system with the Republic of Serbia at the time. I wouldn't go into the parallel system here and now. First of all, as far as the parallel system is concerned, I should ask you whether there were any diplomas that were existence. Were they recognised by universities? What were these parallel schools? Is that not a completely illegitimate thing? Is it not totally out of the education system and outside the state system? My question, the one that I put to you, specifically had to do with elementary school. You mentioned that your daughter went to elementary school and you claimed that there was a wall between the Serbian and the Albanian children in that school, and you claim that in the school there was heating where the Serb children went to school and there was no heating where the Albanian children went to school. Now, my question in relation to this is, first and foremost, what is this elementary school; what is the name of this school? Because, of course, there should be documentation about everything we're discussing. What is your daughter's name? What school did she go to? So that we could obtain the data and see what this was all about. I am truly shocked by what you have said just now. That is what I would be interested in, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: When the school was built it was initially named Marsal Tito. Then when it was separated, I don't know how it was named in the Serbian language because this happened in Milosevic times; but for Albanians we referred to the school with the name of Ismail Qemali. This is the same name we use for this school today. I'm talking here about the period of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Even at that time the Serbian education system did not exist for you. When I say "for you," I'm referring to the Albanian people or nation or Kosovo, since you don't know the name of the school was in the language of the country that at that time had absolute sovereignty over the territory. I am really putting this question to you as a professional and as a legalist.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Since we are entering into a debate over terms, no state that does not have the support of its citizens has no sovereignty. Serbia in Kosova was there through forceful means. It did not have the support of the majority population, and, therefore, it did not enjoy the sovereignty over that territory. Therefore, it's totally irrelevant how that school would be named. That school and that system were imposed by force, and it was that system that divided those children. It divided the children in the worst possible way, by providing funding for some children and discriminating the right of the children -- of other children for education, and it did it through violence. The secondary school pupils were evicted from their schools. The students of Albanian University of Prishtina were forcefully removed from their buildings by the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we must ask you to, if you wish to follow this matter further, to do so on Friday morning. We've run overtime by four minutes now. We will adjourned now to resume on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of January, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
